source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 11: a x b = 0 and a . b = 0 together force a = 0 or b = 0 (book p.283). Answer key PDF 312 agrees.

blocks.prompt: 11. If \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0}\) and \(\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b} = 0\), what conclusion can be drawn about \(\underline{a}\) or \(\underline{b}\)?
blocks.explanation:
A reasoning question.
We must decide what both conditions together force.
Plan: translate each condition into a statement about \(\sin\theta\) or \(\cos\theta\); they cannot both be zero.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0}\) and \(\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b} = 0\).
To find: what must be true of \(\underline{a}\) or \(\underline{b}\).
Method: \(|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}| = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\sin\theta\) and \(\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b} = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\cos\theta\).

Suppose both vectors are non-zero
\[|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\sin\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 0\]
\[|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = 0\]
Why: If \(|\underline{a}| \ne 0\) and \(|\underline{b}| \ne 0\) we may divide by \(|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\). The first says the vectors are parallel, the second that they are perpendicular.

This is impossible
\[\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\]
\[0 + 0 \ne 1\]
Why: No angle has sine and cosine both zero. So the supposition is false.

The same idea in one line
\[|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|^2 + (\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b})^2 = |\underline{a}|^2|\underline{b}|^2\]
\[0 + 0 = |\underline{a}|^2|\underline{b}|^2\]
Why: Adding the squares and using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\). So \(|\underline{a}||\underline{b}| = 0\): \(|\underline{a}| = 0\) or \(|\underline{b}| = 0\).

Check
\[\underline{a} = \underline{0}:\ \underline{0} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0},\ \underline{0} \cdot \underline{b} = 0\]
Why: The zero vector really does satisfy both conditions (it is both parallel and perpendicular to every vector), so the conclusion is possible and is the only one.
blocks.final_answer: At least one of the vectors \(\underline{a}\) or \(\underline{b}\) is the zero vector.
